title: Managing Thermal Expansion And Electromigration Through Interposer Design
gist: As AI-driven bandwidth demand pushes chipmakers toward denser 2.5D and 3D packaging, thermomechanical stress from mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion and rising electromigration risk are becoming the dominant reliability bottlenecks, prompting new deep-learning surrogate models to make warpage prediction computationally tractable.

themes.theme: Why 2.5D interposers are gaining favor over 3D stacking

insights.claim: 3D packages using hybrid bonding achieve the highest interconnect density by stacking active chips vertically, but this creates severe heat dissipation problems because stacked-chip surface area grows more slowly than active device volume, and heat can cause through-silicon vias (TSVs) to expand and crack or delaminate.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: 3D stacking's density advantage comes with compounding thermal and reliability risk, which is pushing some AI chip packaging designs toward the more thermally tractable 2.5D interposer approach instead.
insights.locator: Currently, hybrid bonding achieves the highest available interconnect density

insights.claim: 2.5D packages, which place chips on a passive interposer with wiring rather than active transistors, are simpler to model and manufacture and avoid some of the reliability issues of 3D packages, though a change to one component chip's pad layout still requires redesigning the interposer.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: 2.5D remains the more pragmatic near-term packaging path for AI accelerators needing high interconnect density without the full reliability burden of 3D stacking, favoring interposer and substrate suppliers.
insights.locator: In contrast, 2.5D packages offer a more flexible option.

themes.theme: Thermomechanical failure is the leading 2.5D reliability risk

insights.claim: Researchers at Seoul National University (Hakjun Kim and colleagues) found that thermomechanical failure is the most challenging reliability issue for 2.5D packages, driven by mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) between silicon/copper components (low CTE) and organic substrate, molding compound, and underfill materials (high CTE).
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: CTE mismatch is identified as the single biggest reliability bottleneck in the packaging architecture that AI chipmakers are increasingly relying on, making thermomechanical modeling and materials selection a critical, potentially yield-limiting capability for advanced packaging suppliers.

insights.claim: In multi-chip 2.5D packages, stiffening the package in one area to reduce warpage does not eliminate stress but transfers it elsewhere, potentially causing the interposer-to-substrate bond to fail or redistribution layers to delaminate instead.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: This is a non-obvious engineering trade-off: point fixes for warpage can create new failure modes elsewhere in the package, meaning reliable 2.5D design requires holistic, whole-package stress modeling rather than local optimization.
insights.locator: Kim explained that stiffening the package in one area can increase stress in other areas.

insights.claim: A finite element model from South China University of Technology (Ming-Sheng Luo and colleagues) of a two-chip 2.5D package identified the space between chips and the interposer-to-molding-compound connection as the most failure-prone regions, and found that adding dummy silicon coupons to larger packages can help balance internal stresses.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: Identifying specific failure-prone geometric regions gives packaging engineers concrete design targets (inter-chip spacing, dummy die placement) to mitigate warpage risk in multi-chip 2.5D modules, relevant to AI accelerator packaging yield.
insights.locator: Ming-Sheng Luo and colleagues at South China University of Technology

insights.claim: Moisture absorption by package materials can also drive expansion-related stress, and a given material's hygroscopic (moisture) behavior does not necessarily track its thermal expansion behavior, adding an independent variable to warpage modeling.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: Warpage models that account only for thermal CTE mismatch may miss moisture-driven failure modes, an underappreciated reliability risk in humid or long-field-life environments for 2.5D AI packages.

themes.theme: Electromigration risk rises with interconnect density

insights.claim: Electromigration, historically not a major concern for logic and memory devices, is becoming more relevant as current density in packages rises with increasing interconnect density; researchers at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University found that varying copper electroplating chemistry to produce nanotwinned rather than nanocrystalline grain structure substantially improves electromigration resistance.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
entities: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
insights.so_what: Copper microstructure engineering (nanotwinned vs. nanocrystalline grains) is emerging as a low-cost lever to improve interconnect reliability without adding process complexity like trench liners or alloy dopants, relevant to advanced packaging process suppliers.

insights.claim: Nanocrystalline copper actually reduced electromigration resistance because grain boundaries facilitated diffusion, while nanotwinned copper with a strong (111) texture and coherent twin boundaries (especially after annealing) suppressed oxide formation and void generation.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: This is a counterintuitive, specific finding: finer/different grain structures are not uniformly better for reliability, so redistribution-layer process recipes matter as much as the choice of copper as a material.
insights.locator: In Lin's study, nanocrystalline copper actually reduced electromigration resistance

insights.claim: In situ studies at ASE Group found that redistribution layer (RDL) lines with smaller copper grains achieved lifetimes approximately seven times longer than lines with larger grains.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: A 7x lifetime difference from grain size alone is a large, actionable reliability lever for RDL process engineering at packaging houses like ASE, directly relevant to yield and warranty risk in dense AI packaging.
insights.locator: Smaller grains achieved lifetimes approximately seven times longer than lines with larger grains.

themes.theme: Modeling complexity is driving AI-based surrogate models

insights.claim: The scale mismatch between individual micron-level bond pads and overall multi-chip packages makes full finite element analysis computationally prohibitive, so researchers are beginning to develop deep learning surrogate models as a practical pathway to scalable warpage prediction.
insights.speaker: Katherine Derbyshire
insights.so_what: AI/ML-based surrogate modeling is becoming a necessary tool (not just a nice-to-have) for advanced packaging design, opening a niche EDA/simulation software opportunity for vendors who can deliver validated warpage-prediction ML models.
